newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ rate plan needs rethink, bankers say.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ rate plan needs rethink, bankers say.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand may have to rethink its recent proposal to introduce an official cash rate, meant to bring it in line with other countries, leading banking figures said on Wednesday.
A number of key institutions and senior bankers are against changing New Zealand's unique system where the market currently sets rates, negating the need for an official rate.
"If it ain't broke, don't fix it," was a widespread view of bankers cavassed by Reuters.
RBNZ Governor Don Brash has predicted an announcement will be made in early May following several weeks of consultations.
"With the system now so close to operating well again, why the change?" National Bank chief economist Adrian Orr said.
"The beauty of the present system is that most of the time it is virtually on automatic pilot."

Orr said the proposed system would reduce transparency and flexibility -- contrary to the RBNZ's stated aims. It would increase volatility, particularly in the exchange rate, as evident in other countries using official cash rate systems.

"All these things may not be extremely strong arguments against a cash rate but if you take them all together they add up to a fair bit of scepticism," said another opponent, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Bank chief economist Ulf Schoefisch.
"If you then look at the advantages of a cash rate system, you wonder if the cost-benefits hold up", he added.
In early March, the RBNZ published a disussion paper that proposed scrapping the daily cash settlement target in favour of an official cash rate which would be set after a weekly meeting.
It also suggested scrapping daily float tenders and RB Bills in favour of a more conventional overnight repo system.
The change would move the bank from a system targeting the volume of money in the banking system, via a daily target for settlement cash, to a price-based system.
Opposition to a new system extends into the RBNZ, bankers say. Market opposition does not extend to the planned repo system nor is it totally universal.
WestpacTrust Financial Markets General Manager, Stephen Moir, supports the thrust of proposed change.
"We think targeting the rates rather than the volume is a bit more accurate and brings it in line with what's happening in most markets overseas," he said.
The RBNZ has said a change would give it greater leverage to adjust conditions and increase its ability to correctly read market expectations of its actions.
However, National Bank's Orr disagreed with the notion that markets currently struggle to decipher policy preferences.
"Any recent misunderstandings... are more the result of the wrong use of the monetary signalling device rather the device itself," he said.
ANZ Bank Treasurer Grant Spencer warned that changing the policy mechanism could also raise communication risks.
"In a situation (under the new system) where policy was following the market they would have to be more active and they would have a higher profile than I think is really necessary.
"It would present problems if the RBNZ increased their profile and potentially that could damage credibility if they made slips along the way," Spencer said.
DBMG's Schoefisch, who like Spencer is a former senior RBNZ executive, also opposes a new rate as a signalling tool.
He said there had been few instances in the past five to six years where the market challenged the RBNZ and doubted it was worth manipulating the cash rate all the time to counter that.
"Potentially there is an adjustment frequency of once a week," he added, although the RBNZ has said that in practice it would only expect to make changes once every six to eight weeks.
